items.articleTextTr: ECB'de başkanlık yarışı: Fransa ve Almanya görev dağılımında anlaşmaya yakın - Fransa ve Almanya'nın Avrupa Merkez Bankasının üst düzey yönetim görevlerinin dağılımında anlaşmaya yaklaştığı bildirildi. İspanya Merkez Bankasının eski Başkanı Pablo Hernández de Cos, ECB başkanlığı için öne çıkan aday olarak gösteriliyor. Avrupa Merkez Bankası (ECB) Başkanlığı için İspanya Merkez Bankasının eski Başkanı Pablo Hernández de Cos'un adı öne çıkarken, Fransa ve Almanya'nın bankanın üst düzey yönetim kadrosundaki görev dağılımı konusunda anlaşmaya yakın olduğu bildirildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Euronews'ün haberine göre, AB liderleri Dublin'de düzenlenen gayriresmi zirvede ECB Başkanlığı için iki adayın bulunduğu konusunda bilgilendirildi. Adayların, İspanyol ekonomist Pablo Hernández de Cos ile Hollanda Merkez Bankasının eski Başkanı Klaas Knot olduğu belirtildi. Eurogroup, iki adaylığı geçen hafta teyit etmişti. İspanya'nın El País gazetesi, Fransa ve Almanya'nın ECB'nin üst düzey görevleri konusunda anlaşmayı sonuçlandırmaya yaklaştığını ve de Cos'un başkanlık için öne çıktığını yazdı. Avrupa Konseyi Başkanı António Costa'nın cuma sabahı liderlere süreç hakkında bilgi verdiği, 26 Kasım'daki AB zirvesinde Avrupa Parlamentosu ve ECB Yönetim Konseyi ile istişareleri başlatmayı hedeflediği aktarıldı. Görev dağılımında Almanya ve Fransa pazarlığı Almanya Başbakanı Friedrich Merz ile Fransa Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel Macron'un adaylar üzerinde yoğun görüşmeler yürüttüğü belirtildi. Merz, Dublin'de gazetecilere yaptığı açıklamada anlaşmanın yakın olduğunu ancak henüz kesinleşmediğini söyledi. Almanya'nın önerisini gelecek hafta sunmadan önce koalisyon ortaklarıyla birkaç gün daha istişare etmesi gerektiğini belirtti. El País'in haberine göre Fransa, eski İspanya Merkez Bankası Başkanı de Cos'un ECB başkanlığına getirilmesini destekliyor. De Cos'un para politikasındaki daha ılımlı yaklaşımının, mali baskılarla karşı karşıya olan Fransa açısından uygun görüldüğü ifade edildi. Alman ekonomi gazetesi Handelsblatt'a göre olası anlaşma kapsamında Almanya, ECB'nin başekonomistlik görevini; Fransa ise Isabel Schnabel'in yürüttüğü piyasa operasyonlarından sorumlu üyelik görevini alacak. Almanya'nın başekonomistlik görevi için Princeton Üniversitesi ekonomisti Markus Brunnermeier'i istediği belirtildi. Görev, ECB'nin günlük işleyişini yürüten altı üyeli Yönetim Kurulu'ndaki en önemli pozisyonlardan biri olarak değerlendiriliyor. Klaas Knot'un başkanlığa getirilmesi halinde ise Fransa'nın başekonomistlik görevini, Almanya'nın da piyasa operasyonlarından sorumlu üyeliği üstlenmesinin öngörüldüğü aktarıldı. Alman hükümetinden bir sözcü, Berlin'in ECB yönetiminde "uygun" düzeyde temsil edilmesini istediğini ve yıl sonuna kadar anlaşmaya varılmasını beklediğini söyledi. ECB yönetiminde üç koltuk değişecek ECB Yönetim Kurulu'ndaki görev dağılımı, önümüzdeki aylarda yaşanacak ayrılıklar nedeniyle önem kazanıyor. Isabel Schnabel'in 3 Ocak'ta Uluslararası Para Fonu'nda (IMF) görev almak üzere ECB'den ayrılması bekleniyor. Ayrıca başekonomist Philip Lane'in görev süresi mayıs ayında sona erecek. Bu gelişmelerle birlikte ECB Yönetim Kurulu'nun altı üyesinden üçünün beş aydan kısa sürede görevden ayrılması öngörülüyor. Öte yandan Hernández de Cos'un ECB başkanlığına getirilmesi, 1 Temmuz 2025'ten bu yana genel müdürlüğünü yürüttüğü Uluslararası Ödemeler Bankasında (BIS) da yeni bir üst düzey pozisyonun boşalmasına yol açacak. İsviçre'nin Basel kentinde bulunan ve merkez bankalarının sahibi olduğu BIS, merkez bankalarının bankası olarak anılıyor. De Cos'un ayrılması halinde yerine gelecek ismi BIS Yönetim Kurulu belirleyecek. ECB'nin altı üyeli Yönetim Kurulu'ndaki diğer iki boş pozisyon için aday gösterme sürecinde son tarih 18 Kasım olarak belirlendi. items.titleTr: RWA protocol stUSDT winds down three years after $2.3B TVL peak
items.summaryTr: The stUSDT team did not disclose a reason for winding down the RWA protocol but assured holders that all underlying assets remain fully backed.
items.articleText: RWA protocol stUSDT winds down three years after $2.3B TVL peak The stUSDT team did not disclose a reason for winding down the RWA protocol but assured holders that all underlying assets remain fully backed. Real-world asset (RWA) protocol stUSDT has begun winding down operations, nearly three years after reaching a $2.3 billion total value locked (TVL), ending rewards and opening a six-month redemption window for tokenholders. The team said that interest accrual on stUSDT ended on Saturday, with holders of stUSDT and its wrapped version, wstUSDT, able to redeem through its official portal until May 14, 2027. The team said requests submitted after the deadline will be handled through customer support in monthly batches through August 2027. The team did not provide a reason for the shutdown but said all underlying assets remain fully backed. Holders with tokens on exchanges or DeFi platforms must transfer them to personal wallets before redeeming. Cointelegraph reached out to stUSDT for more information but did not receive a response before publication. Meanwhile, JustLend DAO said it would phase out supply and borrowing functions for its wstUSDT market as part of the transition. Launched in July 2023 on Tron, stUSDT allowed users to deposit USDT and earn yields from investments in real-world assets, including short-term government bonds. The protocol later expanded to Ethereum. According to DefiLlama data, stUSDT’s TVL peaked at about $2.3 billion in November 2023 before declining substantially in subsequent years. It stood at about $8.6 million on Sunday, down from roughly $60 million a year earlier. Despite its name, stUSDT is not affiliated with stablecoin issuer Tether. In September 2023, Tether denied any affiliation with stUSDT, saying the protocol was an independent project. Related: Tron and Tether bring in Chainalysis after T3 crime unit folds

items.articleText: Avrupa'da en çok hangi mesleklerde eleman açığı yaşanıyor? OECD açıkladı - OECD'nin 27 Avrupa ülkesini kapsayan araştırmasına göre öğretmenlik, eleman bulmanın en zor olduğu meslek grubu. Öğretmenleri sağlık profesyonelleri ve bilişim uzmanları izlerken, işçi ve gıda hazırlama personeli pozisyonları daha kolay dolduruluyor. Avrupa'da öğretmenlik, sağlık ve bilişim teknolojileri alanındaki meslekler eleman bulmakta en çok zorlanılan işler arasında yer alırken, işçi ve gıda hazırlama personeli pozisyonları daha kolay dolduruluyor. OECD verilerine göre, meslek gruplarındaki açıklar ülkelerin ekonomik yapısına ve çalışma koşullarına göre değişiyor. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Ekonomik İşbirliği ve Kalkınma Örgütü'nün (OECD) 27 Avrupa ülkesini kapsayan araştırmasına göre, öğretmenlik Avrupa genelinde doldurulması en zor meslek olarak öne çıkıyor. Öğretmenleri sağlık profesyonelleri ile bilgi ve iletişim teknolojileri (BİT) uzmanları izliyor. Sağlık alanındaki yardımcı profesyoneller ile işletme ve yönetim uzmanları da eleman bulmakta zorlanılan ilk beş meslek grubu arasında bulunuyor. Araştırmada işçi pozisyonları doldurulması en kolay işler olarak sıralanırken, bunları temel işlerde çalışanlar, gıda hazırlama personeli, satış çalışanları ve montaj işçileri takip ediyor. OECD'nin endeksi, meslek gruplarındaki açıkları ülke bazında karşılaştırıyor. Pozitif puanlar göreli iş gücü açığına, negatif puanlar ise göreli iş gücü fazlasına işaret ediyor. Endeks, doğrudan açık pozisyon veya eksik çalışan sayısını göstermiyor. Veriler çoğu ülke için 2024 yılına dayanıyor. Öğretmen ve sağlık çalışanı bulmak zorlaşıyor Öğretmenlik, incelenen 27 ülkenin 21'inde eleman bulmakta zorlanılan meslekler arasında yer alıyor. 5 ülkede ise öğretmen arzı ve talebi genel olarak dengeli. Bu ülkeler Almanya, Yunanistan, İtalya, Norveç ve İspanya. Avrupa Eğitim İşverenleri Federasyonu Genel Sekreteri Daniel Wisniewski, öğretmen açığının artık yalnızca boş kadroların doldurulmasıyla ilgili olmadığını, mesleğin uzun vadede cazibesini ve sürdürülebilirliğini de ilgilendirdiğini belirtti. Rekabetçi ücretlerin önemini koruduğunu kaydeden Wisniewski, dijital araçların kullanımı, sınıflarda kapsayıcılığın artırılması, öğrencilerin refahına yönelik sorumluluklar ve idari iş yükünün öğretmenlik mesleğini daha karmaşık hale getirdiğini ifade etti. Wisniewski, çalışma koşulları, mesleki özerklik, kariyer gelişimi ve okul yönetiminin niteliğinin de öğretmenlerin mesleğe yönelmesinde ve meslekte kalmasında belirleyici olduğunu vurguladı. Sağlık profesyonelleri 27 ülkenin 23'ünde, sağlık alanındaki yardımcı profesyoneller ise 21'inde eleman bulmakta zorlanılan meslek grupları arasında bulunuyor. Avrupa Hemşireler Birlikleri Federasyonu temsilcileri Paul De Raeve ve Manuel Ballotta, hemşire açığının temel nedenleri arasında yüksek hasta-hemşire oranını, güvenli olmayan çalışma koşullarını ve ruh sağlığı sorunlarını gösterdi. Temsilciler, düşük ücret, sınırlı kariyer olanakları, mesleki tanınma eksikliği ile taciz ve şiddet olaylarının da hemşirelik mesleğinin cazibesini azalttığını belirtti. Avrupa Doktorları Daimi Komitesi Başkanı Ole Johan Bakke ise doktorların sistemdeki personel açığını aşırı çalışma saatleri ve artan iş yüküyle telafi etmek zorunda kaldığını söyledi. Bakke, sağlık çalışanlarına yönelik şiddetin de tükenmişliği artırarak hekimlik mesleğini uzun vadeli bir kariyer olarak daha az cazip hale getirdiğini ifade etti. Yapay zeka bilişim alanındaki talebi değiştirebilir Bilgi ve iletişim teknolojileri uzmanları ile işletme ve yönetim profesyonelleri, 18'er ülkede eleman bulmakta zorlanılan meslek grupları arasında yer aldı. OECD ekonomisti Isabel Skak Olufsen, dijitalleşmenin bilişim uzmanlarına yönelik talebi artırdığını, ancak yapay zekadaki gelişmelerin gelecekte bazı bilişim pozisyonlarına olan ihtiyacı azaltabileceğini belirtti. Olufsen, özellikle kariyerinin başındaki çalışanlara yönelik pozisyonların bu değişimden etkilenebileceğine dikkati çekti. Ülkelerin ekonomik yapısı iş gücü açığını belirliyor OECD verileri, Avrupa genelindeki eğilimlerin ülkeler arasında farklılaştığını da ortaya koydu. Norveç'te işçi pozisyonları doldurulması en zor işler arasında yer alırken, bu meslek grubu incelenen ülkelerin 21'inde eleman bulmanın daha kolay olduğu alanlardan biri olarak öne çıkıyor. İspanya'da gıda hazırlama personeli, Fransa'da ise temel işlerde çalışanlar eleman bulmakta zorlanılan meslekler arasında bulunuyor. Bilişim alanında da özellikle Kuzey ve Batı Avrupa ülkelerinde farklı bir tablo görülüyor. OECD, Danimarka, Finlandiya, Almanya, Hollanda, Norveç ve İsveç'te bilişim uzmanlarına yönelik iş gücü piyasasını genel olarak dengeli değerlendiriyor. Avusturya, İsviçre ve İngiltere'de ise bu alanda iş gücü fazlasına işaret ediyor. Olufsen, mesleklere yönelik talebin ülkelerin ekonomik yapısına bağlı olarak değiştiğini belirtti. Almanya ve Güney Kore gibi imalat sanayisinin güçlü olduğu ülkelerde montaj işçileri ve makine operatörleri gibi orta beceri gerektiren mesleklerde iş gücü açığının öne çıktığını ifade etti. Avrupa İşgücü Otoritesi (ELA) Sözcüsü Pia-Johanna Fallström ise iş gücü açıklarının giderek geçici olmaktan çıkıp yapısal hale geldiğini belirtti. Fallström, demografik değişim, beceri uyumsuzluğu, iş kalitesi ve sınırlı iş gücü hareketliliğinin bu tabloda etkili olduğunu söyledi. Fallström'e göre Avrupa'nın mesleki eğitim olanaklarını geliştirmesi, çalışma koşullarını iyileştirmesi ve çalışanların becerileriyle işverenlerin ihtiyaçlarını daha iyi eşleştirmesi gerekiyor. Ayrıca, bazı ülkelerde iş gücü fazlası bulunan mesleklerin başka ülkelerdeki açıkları kapatabilmesi için adil iş gücü hareketliliğinin desteklenmesi önem taşıyor.

Olufsen, özellikle kariyerinin başındaki çalışanlara yönelik pozisyonların bu değişimden etkilenebileceğine dikkati çekti. Ülkelerin ekonomik yapısı iş gücü açığını belirliyor OECD verileri, Avrupa genelindeki eğilimlerin ülkeler arasında farklılaştığını da ortaya koydu. Norveç'te işçi pozisyonları doldurulması en zor işler arasında yer alırken, bu meslek grubu incelenen ülkelerin 21'inde eleman bulmanın daha kolay olduğu alanlardan biri olarak öne çıkıyor. İspanya'da gıda hazırlama personeli, Fransa'da ise temel işlerde çalışanlar eleman bulmakta zorlanılan meslekler arasında bulunuyor. Bilişim alanında da özellikle Kuzey ve Batı Avrupa ülkelerinde farklı bir tablo görülüyor. OECD, Danimarka, Finlandiya, Almanya, Hollanda, Norveç ve İsveç'te bilişim uzmanlarına yönelik iş gücü piyasasını genel olarak dengeli değerlendiriyor. Avusturya, İsviçre ve İngiltere'de ise bu alanda iş gücü fazlasına işaret ediyor. Olufsen, mesleklere yönelik talebin ülkelerin ekonomik yapısına bağlı olarak değiştiğini belirtti. Almanya ve Güney Kore gibi imalat sanayisinin güçlü olduğu ülkelerde montaj işçileri ve makine operatörleri gibi orta beceri gerektiren mesleklerde iş gücü açığının öne çıktığını ifade etti. Avrupa İşgücü Otoritesi (ELA) Sözcüsü Pia-Johanna Fallström ise iş gücü açıklarının giderek geçici olmaktan çıkıp yapısal hale geldiğini belirtti. Fallström, demografik değişim, beceri uyumsuzluğu, iş kalitesi ve sınırlı iş gücü hareketliliğinin bu tabloda etkili olduğunu söyledi. Fallström'e göre Avrupa'nın mesleki eğitim olanaklarını geliştirmesi, çalışma koşullarını iyileştirmesi ve çalışanların becerileriyle işverenlerin ihtiyaçlarını daha iyi eşleştirmesi gerekiyor. Ayrıca, bazı ülkelerde iş gücü fazlası bulunan mesleklerin başka ülkelerdeki açıkları kapatabilmesi için adil iş gücü hareketliliğinin desteklenmesi önem taşıyor.

items.articleText: Analist Colombo'dan altında 3400 dolar uyarısı: Haftalık kayıp yüzde 5'e ulaştı Ons altın haftalık bazda yüzde 5 değer kaybederek 3 bin 883,94 dolara geriledi. Analist Jesse Colombo, 3 bin 900 dolarlık desteğin güçlü şekilde kırılması halinde fiyatların 3 bin 400-3 bin 500 dolar bandına çekilebileceği uyarısında bulundu. Altın fiyatlarının ons başına 3 bin 900 dolar seviyesindeki kritik desteği test ettiğini belirten bağımsız değerli metaller analisti Jesse Colombo, bu seviyenin güçlü şekilde kırılması halinde fiyatların 3 bin 400-3 bin 500 dolar bandına gerileyebileceğini öngördü. Kitco News'te yer alan habere göre, bağımsız değerli metaller analisti ve BubbleBubble Report'un kurucusu Jesse Colombo, altın piyasasında daha derin bir düşüş riskinin gündemde olduğunu söyledi. Colombo, altın fiyatları üzerinde doların güçlenmesi, yükselen faiz oranları ve teknoloji hisselerindeki satışların etkili olduğunu belirtti. Altının COMEX vadeli işlemlerinde ons başına yaklaşık 3 bin 900 dolarlık önemli bir destek seviyesinde bulunduğunu kaydeden Colombo, fiyatların bu seviyenin bir miktar altına gerilemesine rağmen henüz net bir kırılma yaşanmadığını ifade etti. Colombo, desteğin kırıldığından emin olmak için fiyatların bu seviyenin belirgin şekilde altına inmesi gerektiğini vurguladı. Analist, altının daha önce de benzer şekilde destek seviyesinin altına sarktığını, zarar-kes emirlerini tetikledikten sonra yeniden toparlandığını hatırlattı. 3 bin 500 dolar seviyesi gündemde Söz konusu destek bölgesinin Ekim-Kasım 2025 dönemindeki dip seviyelerinden bu yana korunduğunu belirten Colombo, altının mart ayında yaşanan sert satışlarda ve haziran-temmuz döneminde de aynı bölgeden destek bulduğunu aktardı. Colombo, ons başına 3 bin 900 dolar civarındaki desteğin güçlü şekilde kırılması halinde altının en az 400 dolar daha değer kaybedebileceğini öngördü. Analist, bu seviyenin altında 3 bin 400-3 bin 500 dolar bandına kadar önemli bir destek boşluğu bulunduğunu belirterek, olası bir kırılmanın ardından fiyatların 3 bin 500 dolar civarına yönelmesini beklediğini söyledi. Doların yükselişi altını baskılıyor Colombo'ya göre altın fiyatlarının yönü üzerinde belirleyici olacak başlıca unsurlardan biri doların seyri. Doların değer kazanmasının değerli metaller üzerinde güçlü bir baskı oluşturduğunu ifade eden Colombo, dolar endeksinin 102-103 seviyelerinin üzerine çıktığına dikkati çekti. Analist, dolar endeksindeki yükseliş ivmesi sona ermeden altın fiyatlarında kalıcı bir dip oluştuğunu söylemekte temkinli davranacağını belirtti. Colombo, doların güçlü yükselişini sürdürmesi halinde altının 3 bin 900 dolar desteğinin altına gerileme ihtimalinin bulunduğunu kaydetti. Ons altın ne kadar? Uluslararası piyasalarda altının onsu, haftalık bazdaki değer kaybının ardından 3 bin 883,94 dolar seviyesinden alıcı buluyor. Piyasa verilerine göre, haftaya 4 bin 120 dolar bandının üzerindeki zirve seviyelerinden başlayan spot altın, hafta genelinde satış baskısıyla karşılaştı. 5 günlük periyotta yüzde 5 oranında değer kaybeden altının onsu, perşembe günü 3 bin 867,76 dolar ile haftanın en düşük seviyesini test etti. Son işlem gününde ise düşüşünü durdurarak tepki alımlarıyla karşılaşan ons altın, 3 bin 876,40 dolar seviyesinden açılış yaptı. Gün içinde 3 bin 867,76 ile 3 bin 923,13 dolar aralığında dalgalanan altının onsu, önceki kapanışa kıyasla 7,48 dolar ve yüzde 0,19 artışla 3 bin 883,94 dolardan kapanış gerçekleştirdi.

items.titleTr: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
items.summaryTr: It is the latest development in a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links.
items.articleText: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation - Published A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations. Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either. Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation. In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline." "The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote. She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings". Her order will last until the 28 November. The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park. The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. The legal fight then escalated in October, when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin. After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes. Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign. "The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post to Truth Social. Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules". That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information. She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

items.articleText: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town - Published On a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat. About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, which is located in a remote part of the Andes mountains in northern Peru, but the Pope's visit drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican. At an outdoor Mass, Pope Leo spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages," and the unequal distribution of the land's resources. Over 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data. Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru. In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties. Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population. On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him. Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again. "It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said. Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz. He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father." The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance. The US-born pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities. The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco, and then on to a Peruvian sector of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point Pope Leo will return to Rome. Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published6 November

items.titleTr: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
items.summaryTr: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
items.articleText: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive - Published When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified. They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. "Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive. This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded. Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry. Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community. After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience. "As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works. The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate. The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team. After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve. Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north. This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance. After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea. This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre. "She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says. Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance. He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. "The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea. In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding. Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified. "I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains. Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok. The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him. However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged. "We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC. For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region. He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance. Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns. "We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC. They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation. After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust. "I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real. But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding. Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says. "Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate". He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion. But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone. Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community. He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly." He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing. "The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says. The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment. Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease. "Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited." items.summary: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.

items.titleTr: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
items.summaryTr: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.
items.articleText: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy - Published Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business. More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him. Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer. So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace? "Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro. "But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes." For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly. But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray. The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May. So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note. It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling. Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!" In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks. All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices. "People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said. "Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool." It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. - Riner equals French gold medal record - Published3 August 2024 But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now. What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine? In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate? Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen. In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes. The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off. Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right. The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February. The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely. So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday. The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals". That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss. Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist". Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way". If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt. Related topics Read more - Published4 days ago - Published6 days ago
items.articleTextTr: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy - Published Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business. More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him. Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer. So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace? "Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro. "But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes." For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly. But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray. The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May. So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note. It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling. Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!" In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks. All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices. "People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said. "Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool." It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. - Riner equals French gold medal record - Published3 August 2024 But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now. What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine? In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate? Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen. In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes. The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off. Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right. The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February. The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely. So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday. The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals". That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss. Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist". Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way". If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. items.titleTr: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
items.summaryTr: Beauty calendars have become a Christmas staple and have become particularly popular with female shoppers.
items.articleText: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money? - Published It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use. "I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid." Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated. High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows, external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out. But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier. "I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist. She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product. "For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales." Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy." Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing". So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to? Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them. "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it. In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.
